```
triton                  3.6.0
```

**The kernel-mode NVIDIA driver version (e.g. `580.xx`) is not captured above** — `cuda_driver_version` is the CUDA driver *API* version. That is the single most useful field for deciding whether this is a fleet change, and it needs to come from `nvidia-smi` / DCGM on the nodes below.

## Hardware / placement

```
cluster        cw-us-east-08a
node type      gb200-4x   (2x NVIDIA Grace Arm v9, 144 vCPU, 960 GB LPDDR5X, 4x Blackwell)
job shape      8 racks x 16 nodes = 128 tasks x 4 GPUs = 512 GPUs
topology       multinode-nvlink-ib, gang-scheduled
```

## Fault coordinates

All times UTC, 2026-08-04. "First fault" is the first `CUDA_ERROR_ILLEGAL_INSTRUCTION` line for that attempt.

| Run | Tree | First fault | Task | Node |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `ras8` | `75d12bd05` | 06:50:24 | 80 | `s38vxs64` |
| `ctrl9` | `75d12bd05` | 08:21:16 | 5 | `s6xvxs64` |
| `norasA` | `75d12bd05` | 14:27:16 | 13 | (available on request) |
| `oldbaseB` | `5e496b051` | 15:28:11 | 86 | (rack 5; RAS shows subnet `10.186.210.0/24` lagging) |

**These four timestamps + nodes are the input for suggestion 2 in https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7344#issuecomment-5181330482** — correlating DCGM / NVML / Xid at these exact moments. An illegal instruction normally raises a driver Xid (13 / 31 / 43 class). A shared Xid signature across four different physical nodes separates a fleet or driver problem from a generated-kernel fault, and is far cheaper than any further 512-GPU run.

## Reproduce

```bash
RID=<run-id>
iris --cluster=marin job run --no-wait --enable-extra-resources \
  --target-cluster cw-us-east-08a --priority production \
  --cpu 2 --memory 8GB --disk 32GB --timeout 21600 \
  --job-name "${RID}-coord" -e WANDB_API_KEY "$WANDB_API_KEY" \
  -- python -m experiments.grug.moe_hero_fsdp.launch \
     --run-id "$RID" --dp-racks 8 --num-steps 200 --version dev --run
```

`--target-cluster cw-us-east-08a` is required: Iris child jobs inherit the parent's region, so without it the GB200 request is pinned to wherever the coordinator landed and comes back `unschedulable: no scaling group provides device gpu:gb200`.

Retrieving the fault requires `--since-ms` timestamp windows rather than `--tail`. During the failure the 128 tasks emit ~15k lines/sec, so the crash is displaced from even a 40,000-line tail within seconds.

## Caveat on the "regression" framing in the title

The fault is **not step-locked and not rank-locked** (steps 23 / 85 / 89 / 146; four different tasks on four different nodes), so a single clean run does not clear a configuration. A pristine `5e496b051` control is in flight now and is currently past every prior fault point — if it completes, the range-regression framing in this issue's title is wrong and I will say so here.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖 **Corrected scope + consolidated repro. This is not a code regression, and the original title was wrong — I have retitled the issue.**

## Correction to the original report

The issue was filed as "regression since `5e496b051`" because that tree had completed 200 steps cleanly twice. That framing is **wrong**: `5e496b051` has since produced the same fault (`oldbaseB`, task 86, step 146). Both trees fail.

Also superseded from the original body: the leading hypothesis was #7951 (NCCL RAS polling). **That is exonerated** — `norasA` ran unmodified `main` with `NCCL_RAS_ENABLE=0` and still faulted. Checkpointing (#7929) is also not necessary: `ras8` faulted ~12 min in at step ~23, before any 30-minute checkpoint could exist.

Supporting the "not in this repo" conclusion: across `5e496b051..75d12bd05`, `model.py` and `heuristic.py` are unchanged, `launch.py` changes are confined to checkpointing/telemetry/watchdog, and **`uv.lock` is unchanged** — so the compiled program and the entire Python/CUDA toolchain are identical between the two trees.

## Full observation matrix

`II` = `CUDA_ERROR_ILLEGAL_INSTRUCTION`. All runs are 8 racks = 128 x GB200x4 = 512 GPUs on `cw-us-east-08a`, 200 steps requested.

| Tree | RAS | Local watchdog | Run | Outcome |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `75d12bd05` | on | yes | `ras8` | **II** — task 80, step ~23 |
| `75d12bd05` | on | no *(pristine)* | `ctrl9` | **II** — task 5, step ~89 |
| `75d12bd05` | off | no *(pristine)* | `norasA` | **II** — task 13, step ~85 |
| `5e496b051` | on | yes | `oldbaseB` | **II** — task 86, step 146 |
| `5e496b051` | on | no *(pristine)* | `oldpureD` | **wedge**, no error (#7344) — step 189 |
| `5e496b051` | on | no | `repro-v3` *(prev. day)* | **wedge**, no error (#7344) — step 182 |
| `5e496b051` | on | no | `obs`, `obs4` *(prev. day)* | clean, 200 steps, x2 |

Every II is from 2026-08-04. The previous day's four runs on `5e496b051` produced one wedge and two clean 200-step runs and **zero** IIs.

**Relationship to #7344 is unresolved.** The signatures are clearly different (II is loud, single-rank, kills the gang; the wedge is silent, all-ranks, hangs indefinitely with zero `CUDA_ERROR` in the full log range). But a single underlying GPU fault that sometimes raises an error and sometimes just stops progressing would explain both, and an II *does* produce a wedge-like downstream state — `oldbaseB`'s RAS snapshot showed one rack lagging with every rank alive and nothing marked dead. I am not claiming these are independent bugs.

## The error

```
jax.errors.JaxRuntimeError: INTERNAL: Failed to retrieve branch_index value on stream 0x…:
  CUDA error: Could not synchronize CUDA stream:
  CUDA_ERROR_ILLEGAL_INSTRUCTION: an illegal instruction was encountered
```

CUDA errors are asynchronous, so the `branch_index` site is only where JAX noticed a poisoned context — the illegal instruction executed in an earlier kernel.

## Environment

Observed on-node, from an NCCL RAS report captured on a live training rank:

```
nccl_version          2.28.9
cuda_driver_version   13020      (CUDA 13.2 driver API)
cuda_runtime_version  13000      (CUDA 13.0 runtime)
```

Pinned in `uv.lock`, identical on both trees:

```
jax / jaxlib          0.11.0        nvidia-nccl-cu13    2.28.9
jax-cuda13-plugin     0.11.0        nvidia-cudnn-cu13   9.19.0.56
jax-cuda13-pjrt       0.11.0        triton              3.6.0
```

Hardware: `cw-us-east-08a`, `gb200-4x` nodes (2x Grace Arm v9, 144 vCPU, 960 GB LPDDR5X, 4x Blackwell), `multinode-nvlink-ib`, gang-scheduled.

## Still missing — and I cannot obtain it

**The kernel-mode NVIDIA driver version (`580.xx`-style) is not recorded anywhere I can reach.** `cuda_driver_version 13020` above is the CUDA driver *API* version, which is not the same thing. I checked `iris.worker` telemetry — it carries `gpu_power_w`, `gpu_temp_c`, `gpu_util_pct`, `hbm_*`, but no driver identity — and `iris process` has no exec, so I cannot run `nvidia-smi` on a node.

This is the single most valuable missing field, because the strongest evidence here is temporal: the same commit ran clean one day and fails the next with an unchanged toolchain. Anyone with node access can settle it with:

```bash
nvidia-smi --query-gpu=driver_version,vbios_version --format=csv
```

Two other useful items in the same vein:

1. **Xid / DCGM at the four fault timestamps below.** An illegal instruction normally raises a driver Xid (13 / 31 / 43 class). A shared Xid across four different physical nodes separates a fleet or driver problem from a generated-kernel fault, and costs no GPU time.
2. **Node image / firmware version history for `cw-us-east-08a`** covering 2026-08-03 ~16:00 UTC → 2026-08-04 ~06:30 UTC, the window between the last clean run and the first failure.

## Fault coordinates

All 2026-08-04 UTC. First `CUDA_ERROR_ILLEGAL_INSTRUCTION` line for the attempt.

| Run | Tree | First fault | Task | Node |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `ras8` | `75d12bd05` | 06:50:24 | 80 | `s38vxs64` |
| `ctrl9` | `75d12bd05` | 08:21:16 | 5 | `s6xvxs64` |
| `norasA` | `75d12bd05` | 14:27:16 | 13 | (not captured) |
| `oldbaseB` | `5e496b051` | 15:28:11 | 86 | (rack 5; RAS shows subnet `10.186.210.0/24` lagging) |

## Reproduce

```bash
RID=<run-id>
git checkout 75d12bd05   # or 5e496b051 — both reproduce
iris --cluster=marin job run --no-wait --enable-extra-resources \
  --target-cluster cw-us-east-08a --priority production \
  --cpu 2 --memory 8GB --disk 32GB --timeout 21600 \
  --job-name "${RID}-coord" -e WANDB_API_KEY "$WANDB_API_KEY" \
  -- python -m experiments.grug.moe_hero_fsdp.launch \
     --run-id "$RID" --dp-racks 8 --num-steps 200 --version dev --run
```

`--target-cluster cw-us-east-08a` is required — Iris child jobs inherit the parent's region, so without it the GB200 request is pinned to wherever the coordinator landed and returns `unschedulable: no scaling group provides device gpu:gb200`.

Retrieve the fault with `--since-ms` timestamp windows, not `--tail`: during the failure the 128 tasks emit ~15k lines/sec, so the crash is displaced from even a 40,000-line tail within seconds.

**Expected detection power.** Fitting a constant per-step hazard to the three main-tree faults gives `p ≈ 0.015/step`, so a 200-step run has roughly a **95%** chance of surfacing this (95% CI on the required length is wide: 66–950 steps). A single clean 200-step run is therefore reasonable but not conclusive evidence of a fix.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖 **Fleet is fully homogeneous — the "cluster changed underneath us" theory is not supported. But the fault rate does differ by tree, so my previous "not a code regression" retitle was also too strong. Both corrected below.**

## Kernel-mode driver version (the field that was missing)

Obtained from CoreWeave node labels via the cluster kubeconfig — no exec required:

```bash
kubectl --kubeconfig ~/.kube/coreweave-iris --context marin-us-east-08a_US-EAST-08A get nodes -o json
```

Across **all 205 GB200 nodes in `cw-us-east-08a`**, every version dimension is identical:

```
kernel                    6.17.13-155-gdec5393c-coreweave-arm64
OS                        Ubuntu 24.04
GPU driver                595.71.05
GPU firmware (all 4)      97.00.B9.00.99
Mellanox NIC fw (all 4)   28.47.2526
ncore image               2.49.0  /  ofed-d30da48-n595-kver6.17-gdec5393c-bundle-arm64
CUDA driver API           13020        CUDA runtime  13000
NCCL                      2.28.9
```

(The only 4 non-GB200 nodes in the cluster are CPU-class; they carry no GPU labels and are unrelated.)

## This undercuts the fleet-change hypothesis

I previously argued the regression was likely a node image / driver / firmware change, because the same commit ran clean on 2026-08-03 and failed on 2026-08-04 with `uv.lock` unchanged. The node labels do not support that:

- **Zero heterogeneity** — one kernel, one driver, one GPU firmware, one NIC firmware, one node image across the entire GB200 fleet.
- The nodes that actually faulted have carried this driver **since their creation in July**: `s38vxs64` created 2026-07-15, `s6xvxs64` created 2026-07-25, `s1nrxs64` created 2026-07-22. Their `nvidia.com/gfd.timestamp` equals their creation time, i.e. the GPU labels were never refreshed by a driver upgrade.
- 16 GB200 nodes *were* created 2026-08-04 13:17–13:28 UTC, but they are autoscaler capacity with **identical** images, and they postdate the first two faults (06:50 and 08:21 UTC).

So unless a driver was swapped in place without the GPU Operator relabelling — which would be unusual — the fleet did not change between the clean runs and the failing ones.

## Correcting my own retitle: the rate does differ by tree

I retitled this issue "not a code regression" on the strength of `5e496b051` also faulting. Looking at rates rather than presence/absence, that was too strong:

| Tree | II events | Exposed steps | rate |
|---|---|---|---|
| `75d12bd05` | 3 | 197 | 0.0152 / step |
| `5e496b051` | 1 | 917 | 0.0011 / step |

**Rate ratio ≈ 14x.** Under a null of equal rates, main would be expected to produce 0.71 events and produced 3; one-sided Poisson gives **p ≈ 0.035**. That is marginal evidence, not proof, but it is enough that a code contribution should not be dismissed.

Exposure accounting: main = the three II runs; old tree = `oldbaseB` (II at 146) plus `oldpureD` (189, wedged), `repro-v3` (182, wedged), `obs` and `obs4` (200 each, clean) as censored observations.

**Caveats, which are substantial at 3 vs 1 events:**

1. Small numbers. The confidence interval on a 14x ratio with four total events is very wide.
2. **Tree and time-of-day are partly confounded.** The main-tree runs are mostly early (06:50, 08:21) and the old-tree runs are late (15:28, 16:47), with `norasA` at 14:27 in between. If anything drifted across the day, it is aliased onto the tree comparison.
3. The old-tree exposure includes the previous day's runs, when conditions may not have been identical.

## Where that leaves it

- The fault is **real on both trees** — a bisect that assumes `5e496b051` is clean will mislead.
- Main is **plausibly much worse**, so the 15-commit range is worth revisiting rather than dismissed. Given `model.py`, `heuristic.py`, and `uv.lock` are all unchanged across it, the mechanism would have to be indirect — scheduling/placement (#7928 makes CPU reservations topology-aware on CoreWeave, which can change NUMA and device affinity) is the most plausible candidate remaining.
- Distinguishing a 14x rate difference from noise needs roughly **4-5 more runs per arm**, which is expensive; the cheaper discriminator is still Xid/DCGM at the four fault timestamps already listed in this issue.

Correcting the title accordingly to reflect both trees and the rate difference.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
## New instance with full all-rank verification: `moe-hero-fsdp-12rack-r25fa4-20260805`

Hit this while running the #7344 ablation ladder. This capture is cleaner than earlier ones
because it brackets the onset exactly rather than post-kill flood — see the capture note at
the bottom.

**Config:** 12 racks (192 nodes / 768 GPUs), `num_layers=1`, `attention_implementation="gpu_fa4_cute"`,
`moe_implementation="sonic_cute"`, `expert_chunks=4`, real data, `offload_opt_state=False`.

### Timeline (cluster time)

| time | rank | event |
|---|---|---|
| 06:01:20 | **all 0–191** | step **300**, loss 4.74, ~1.2 s/step — uniformly healthy |
| 06:01:21.433359 | **78** | `cudaFreeAsync failed to free …: CUDA_ERROR_ILLEGAL_INSTRUCTION` |
| →06:01:22.104668 | 78 | 666 failed `cudaFreeAsync` + 19 failed module unloads = 685 lines, devices [0]–[3] |
| 06:06:22.998317 | 0 | `Shutdown barrier … DEADLINE_EXCEEDED … 1/192 … first task at the barrier: 78` |
| 06:06:23.007 | all | `Terminating process because the JAX distributed service detected fatal errors` |

### All-rank verification

A single bounded query against the training-job parent from 06:01:15 with
`--no-tail --max-lines 100000`, grouped by task, shows:

- step 300 logged by **every** task 0–191;
- **no** task logged step 301;
- all 685 illegal-instruction records came from **task 78 only**;
- no other task produced any CUDA error.

So task 78 is the first and only *logged* GPU fault in the complete retrievable onset window.
(An unreported lower-level failure elsewhere can't be excluded from logs alone.)

### The 300 s is JAX's default shutdown timeout

Last teardown error → barrier expiry = **300.894 s**, which is JAX's default
`shutdown_timeout_seconds=300`. The gang did not hang indefinitely; it waited exactly one
shutdown timeout and aborted.

This gives a **discriminator against #7344**: a #7956 fault self-aborts within ~300 s,
whereas #7344 runs sit with `failures=0` and all tasks alive for far longer (measured:
4883 s, 5590 s, 7203 s). I'd suggest keeping the two issues separate on that basis, while
leaving open that they could share a root cause.

### Notes on attribution

- `cudaFreeAsync` is only where the **sticky, asynchronous** error surfaced — not the
  offending kernel. This capture lacks the explicit `JaxRuntimeError … Failed to retrieve
  branch_index … [executable_name='jit_train_step']` seen in earlier occurrences.
- Allocator `InUse` was 55.20 GiB against a 138.22 GiB limit — **no memory pressure**.
- `InUse` then falls 55.20 → 3.55 GiB → 65 MiB alongside the errors and module unloads:
  an unwind/teardown pattern.
- Errors appear on devices [0]–[3], but that does **not** establish propagation from one
  device — the same executable runs on all four.
- The same executable ran successfully for ~300 steps and has failed on varying ranks across
  occurrences. That argues against a plain architecture/SASS target mismatch and toward a
  data-dependent kernel bug, memory corruption, or a driver/hardware fault.

### Suggested next step

The most informative single run is `moe_implementation="scatter"` **with
`expert_chunks=1`** (required — `_moe/local.py:64` rejects `scatter`/`sonic` unless
`expert_chunks == 1`, so neither is a one-field swap), everything else unchanged. That gives
a stock-XLA MoE control, removing the QuACK/CUTLASS grouped GEMMs.

Worth noting for anyone testing the toolchain: `sonic_cute` depends on `quack-kernels==0.6.1`
and `nvidia-cutlass-dsl==4.6.0`. A NCCL/cuDNN/Triton bump does **not** update those primary
kernel packages.

Highest-value no-GPU action first: correlate node/Xid/DCGM data for task 78 at 06:01:21.433.

### Capture procedure

`iris job logs <TASK path> --level info --since-seconds N --no-tail`

`--no-tail` combined with `--since` returns the **earliest** lines in the window, so it
reaches the fault onset. Plain `--tail` returns the most recent lines, which after a kill or
auto-retry is pure shutdown/setup flood — several of my earlier captures spanned a single
second and were no evidence at all. Also note `--level error` is dominated by `uv` install
output on restart, since uv writes to stderr.

🤖 Filed while investigating #7344; analysis independently reviewed before posting.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
## Node/rack table for all 7 known occurrences, a repeat offender, and a confound that blocks attribution

Two more occurrences today, plus recovered node identities for every earlier one.
**Correction first:** the "first fault 15:28:11" in this issue's body is wrong — that is a
healthy step-137 timestamp. The first retained illegal-instruction record for `oldbaseB` is
**2026-08-04 15:31:32.844856 UTC** on `s7htxs64`.

### All known occurrences with node identity

Recovered by joining Iris's retained `task_attempts.node_name` against the node inventory:

| run | rank | node / IP | physical rack | mesh position |
|---|---:|---|---|---|
| `ctrl9` | 5 | `s6xvxs64` / `10.186.213.49` | r392 | replica 0, data 20–23 |
| `norasA` | 13 | `sj1txs64` / `10.186.213.67` | r392 | replica 0, data 52–55 |
| `oldbaseB` | 86 | `s7htxs64` / `10.186.210.235` | r129 | replica 5, data 24–27 |
| `ras8` | 80 | `s38vxs64` / `10.186.210.229` | r129 | replica 5, data 0–3 |
| `rasB` | 136 | `s9xvxs64` / `10.186.210.195` | r128 | replica 8, data 32–35 |
| `r25fa4` | 78 | `sjwsxs64` / `10.186.207.87` | **r122** | replica 4, data 56–59 |
| `r3nopgle` | 75 | `sgd50t64` / `10.186.207.109` | **r122** | replica 4, data 44–47 |

**All seven fault nodes are distinct.** Rack counts: r392=2, r129=2, r128=1, r122=2. So there
is no single universally-bad rack across history — but several two-event rack/mesh pairs.

### A repeat offender within one job

`moe-hero-fsdp-12rack-r3nopgle-20260805` died twice, and **rank 75 (`sgd50t64`) is implicated
in both**:

- crash 1 (step 7): 4902 `CUDA_ERROR_ILLEGAL_INSTRUCTION` lines, **all from rank 75**
- crash 2 (step 110): `Shutdown barrier … 1/192`, **first task at the barrier: 75** (no
  illegal-instruction record inside the captured window)

Iris reuses the same allocation across retries, so this is the same physical node twice.

### The confound that blocks attribution

`r25fa4` and `r3nopgle` used **the identical 192 nodes at identical task indices**. And the
mesh is built by reshaping global `jax.devices()` straight into
`(replica_dcn, data, expert, model)` (`lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/sharding.py:168`), so
with 1 process × 4 GPUs per task:

```
replica_dcn = rank // 16
```

**Ranks 64–79 are simultaneously the whole physical r122 slice AND the entire logical
`replica_dcn=4` slice.** The scheduler makes 16-rank topology slices contiguous by task
ordinal (`lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/backends/k8s/tasks.py:931`), and its rack ordering was
stable, so replica 4 repeatedly landed on r122.

That matters because batches are sharded over `("replica_dcn", "data", "expert")` and the
loader selects examples from the device sharding map
(`lib/levanter/src/levanter/data/loader.py:202`) — **replica 4 sees different examples and
different MoE routing than other replicas.** A data-dependent kernel bug and a bad rack are
currently indistinguishable. (The two faults did occupy different `data` quartets, so it is
at least not one exact repeated data coordinate.)

I found no special-casing of ranks 64–79 or replica 4 in the code; only rank 0 is the JAX
coordinator, and the compiled SPMD program is symmetric across `replica_dcn`.

### On the statistics — I want to be explicit that these are weak

I initially computed `(16/192)² = 0.7%`. **That is the wrong reference class**: it assumes the
rack was named before either fault. Honest numbers:

- same rack, *after* the first fault identified r122: **1/12 = 8.3%**
- any rack collecting ≥2 of the three 12-rack faults (r128, r122, r122): **23.6%**
- same `/24` collision, using the actual unequal subnet sizes: **31.9%**

And the two runs are not independent allocation trials — same fleet, same rank mapping. So:
**suggestive operational signal, weak statistical evidence.** It justifies telemetry and a
provisional quarantine, not a declaration that r122 is bad.

### Asks

1. **Xid / DCGM telemetry** at the seven node/timestamp coordinates above — per-GPU Xids,
   SXid/NVLink errors, ECC, row-remap/retired pages, resets, DCGM diagnostics. This is the
   most perishable evidence and the highest-value next step. Application logs contain no Xid
   or DCGM records, so this has to come from the fleet side.
2. **Either** temporarily quarantine `DH1-122-US-EAST-08A`, **or** rotate the
   topology-domain ordering so `replica_dcn=4` lands on different hardware. The rotation is
   the better experiment: it de-aliases rack from mesh position. If the fault follows
   replica 4 to new hardware, the hardware theory dies.

There appears to be no user-facing placement/exclusion control for this: `ResourceConfig`
exposes region/zone/cluster/device but not rack or node
(`lib/fray/src/fray/types.py:413`), and while the Iris protobuf can express `NE`, the K8s
backend only translates `EQ` for known `pool`/`region` keys — rack is not mapped
(`.../k8s/tasks.py:306`). So this needs cluster ops.

### Impact on the #7344 ladder

A #7956 crash is a **competing risk** that right-censors an ablation rung — it is not
evidence the rung does or does not wedge. Two rungs in a row have now been censored (rung 2.5
at step 300, rung 3 at steps 7 and 110), so I am pausing advancement to later rungs rather
than reading censored runs as results.

🤖 Node identities recovered and statistics corrected via independent review.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
## Correction to my previous comment: `moe_implementation="scatter"` has already been tested

In [my earlier comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7956#issuecomment-5188810589) I
proposed `moe_implementation="scatter"` + `expert_chunks=1` as the "most informative single
run", on the premise that the QuACK/CUTLASS MoE path had never been ablated.

**That premise was wrong.** It was ablated, in rung 1 of the #7344 ladder. Provenance from
that run:

```
[provenance] model: num_layers=1 attn=reference moe=scatter expert_chunks=1 sconv=True rope_fused=True vocab=128256 seq=4096
```

So the suggested "control" configuration has already run — and it **wedged** (#7344, step 78,
twice). I asserted it was untested by reading the current working-tree config instead of the
provenance line, which is exactly what that line exists to prevent.

### What the existing data does and does not say

**For #7344 (the wedge):** both vendored CuTe families are already excluded as *necessary*
causes — the wedge reproduces with `attn=reference` **and** `moe=scatter`.

**For #7956 (this issue):** the run is still weakly informative, because the endpoints differ.
Every illegal-instruction fault observed so far occurred with `gpu_fa4_cute` + `sonic_cute`
active; none has been seen under `reference` + `scatter`:

| config | II faults | note |
|---|---|---|
| `gpu_fa4_cute` + `sonic_cute` | 7 occurrences | ctrl9, norasA, oldbaseB, ras8, rasB, r25fa4, r3nopgle |
| `reference` + `scatter` | 0 | r1recap, l1, l1b, r1stockb |

But those rung-1 runs accumulated only a few hundred steps before wedging, so at the observed
fault rate the expected count is order-1. **Absence there is suggestive, not exculpatory**, and
I should not have implied a clean control existed either way.

### Revised suggestion

A dedicated `reference` + `scatter` run held to a pre-declared exposure would make that row
meaningful, but it is expensive and the wedge will keep ending the runs early. The better
target is the un-ablated remainder — **`sconv=True` and `rope_fused=True` were active in rung 1**
and have never been varied in any run.

Separately, `CUDA_LAUNCH_BLOCKING=1` appears to **suppress** the fault rather than localise it
(0 faults in 1185 steps vs 3 in 417 without it), so it cannot serve as an attribution tool
here. Explicit synchronisation boundaries around attention / MoE / loss / optimizer — the other
half of @rjpower's [suggestion](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7344#issuecomment-5181330482)
— preserve kernel overlap and remain the more promising route.

🤖 Correcting my own error rather than leaving a wrong premise in the thread.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖 **Five more faults today at 4 racks with `sonic_cute`, with reconstructed coordinates for @ClassicLarry's report above.**

Following up on [larry's report](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7956#issuecomment-5246921481). I pulled the retained Iris attempt records and logs for both `mhep-ctxext-d2048-fsdp-chunk4-to-fsdp-chunk1` jobs: five distinct single-rank faults, four of them consecutive attempts of one job.

Config, read from the W&B run config rather than a working tree:

```
attention_implementation  gpu_fa4_cute     moe_implementation  sonic_cute
expert_chunks             1                capacity_factor     1.0
hidden_dim 2048   num_layers 22   num_experts 128   top-k 4   num_shared_experts 2
max_seq_len 65536   sliding_window 2048
replica_axis_size 4   expert_axis_size 1   train_batch_size 256  (16.8M tokens/step)
offload_opt_state False   enable_pgle False
```

## Fault coordinates

Onset is the first `CUDA_ERROR_ILLEGAL_INSTRUCTION` line of the attempt. Every event is single-rank: no other task emitted a CUDA error anywhere in the window.

| Job | Attempt | Onset (UTC) | Rank | Node | Attempt ended |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `…-20260810` | 0 | 17:05:12 | 14 | `sgzvxs64` | 17:10:25 |
| `…-20260810b` | 0 | 17:46:57 | 2 | `s5trxs64` | 17:52:09 |
| `…-20260810b` | 1 | 18:13:31 | 2 | `s5trxs64` | 18:18:47 |
| `…-20260810b` | 2 | 18:57:01 | 2 | `s5trxs64` | 19:02:15 |
| `…-20260810b` | 3 | 19:18:35 | 4 | `s8rrxs64` | killed by user |

The 300 s mechanism reproduces exactly. Attempt 0's fault at 17:46:57 produced `Shutdown barrier in coordination service has failed … The first task at the barrier: 2` at 17:51:59, 302 s later. The teardown shape matches too — the 19:18:35 event emitted 2481 `failed to unload module`, 920 `cudaFreeAsync`, and 132 `Error destroying CUDA event` lines in under a second, all from the one rank.

## Three corrections to the reproduction section

**4 racks reproduce it.** Every prior event was 8 or 12 racks. At 256 GPUs this is a third the cost of the 8-rack recipe currently in the description.

**`expert_chunks=1` reproduces it.** All nine prior faults ran `expert_chunks=4`, so chunking is not necessary.

**The model shape is not load-bearing.** d2048 / 22 layers / seq 65536 faults the same way as the hero's d6144 / 48 layers / seq 4096.

The hazard is also much higher here than the ~0.015/step the body fits: four consecutive attempts, each dying after 100–500 steps.

## A trap for anyone building the Xid table

In none of the four attempts does the Iris-recorded failed task match the faulting rank. Iris marks rank 0 (`exit_code 133`, node `s1wvxs64`) in three of them and rank 13 in the fourth; those are the coordinator and a barrier casualty, not the rank that executed the illegal instruction. The faulting ranks — 14, 2, 2, 4 — come only from the logs. Correlating Xid against the `task_attempts.state=5` node would point at the wrong hardware.

## Repeat offender, with the usual confound

`s5trxs64` faulted three consecutive times. Attempts 0–2 reused one allocation, so rank 2 and `s5trxs64` are perfectly confounded — the same aliasing described in [this comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7956#issuecomment-5188810589). Attempt 3 drew a fresh allocation and faulted on rank 4 on a different node, so the fault did not follow mesh position 2 onto new hardware. That is one observation, and it points away from a purely data-dependent explanation.

## Concurrent control without `sonic_cute`

`mhep-hero-d6144-sw2048-20T-10r-watch-20260810` ran on the same fleet in the same window: 10 racks / 640 GPUs, `gpu_fa4_cute` with `moe_implementation="fixed_all_to_all"`, 48 layers, d6144. Clean past step 175 and still running. An earlier 640-GPU run of the same family reached step 435 before larry killed it, also clean. Neither emitted the signature.

That exposure is far too small to clear the FA4 path — at the historical rate the expected count is order-1, the same objection that applies to the rung-1 rows. It is worth recording only because it is the FA4-without-`sonic_cute` path running clean on the same cluster, on the same day, while every `sonic_cute` attempt faulted.

## Capture recipe

`iris query "SELECT task_id, attempt_id, state, node_name FROM task_attempts WHERE task_id LIKE '…'"` recovers per-attempt `node_name` from the controller DB with no cluster access, including for attempts that were later killed. For logs, `--no-tail --since-ms <onset minus 60s>` reaches the onset; the fault emits ~3.5k error lines in well under a second, so `--tail` misses it, and a window that starts before training begins fills the line cap with `uv` install output on stderr.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖 **This reproduces on 1 rack / 64 GPUs. The 8-rack recipe in the description is 8x larger than it needs to be.**

Building on the 4-rack `ctxext` faults [above](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7956#issuecomment-5247127430), I ran that shape down the rack ladder. It faulted at one rack, with `replica_axis_size=1`.

```
[rank0] E0811 02:30:45.245461  cuda_event.cc:50] CUDA error: Error destroying CUDA event:
        CUDA_ERROR_ILLEGAL_INSTRUCTION: an illegal instruction was encountered
```

| | |
|---|---|
| Run | `ii-repro-1rack-b-20260811-0215` (W&B `marin-community/marin_moe`) |
| Shape | 1 rack, 16 nodes, **64 GPUs**, `replica_axis_size=1`, `expert_axis_size=1` |
| Onset | 2026-08-11 02:30:45.245 UTC, ~36 s after the first step, before step 1 was logged |
| Faulting rank | iris task 14, local rank 0 = global JAX rank 56, node `sg8txs64` |
| Signature | 3473 lines: 2393 `failed to unload module`, 664 `cudaFreeAsync`, 399 CUDA-event destroys, 17 host-memory unregisters |
| Isolation | only task 14 emitted any CUDA error; the other 15 tasks were clean |
| Gang death | `local rank 0 exited with code -6` at 02:35:50 — **305 s** after onset |
| Final state | `failures=1`, `failed=1`, `cosched_failed=15` |

Same mechanism as every prior occurrence, at an eighth of the hardware: one rank takes a device-side
fault, its context is destroyed, it reaches the shutdown barrier alone, and one 300 s JAX timeout
later the gang dies.

## What this retires

At `replica_axis_size=1` there are no cross-rack DCN collectives in the program at all. The
multi-rack explanations in this thread cannot be the mechanism:

- the r122 quarantine proposal and the "one bad rack" framing;
- the `replica_dcn=4` / rank-64-79 mesh aliasing described in
  [this comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7956#issuecomment-5188810589);
- the `s5trxs64` repeat-offender confound from the 4-rack runs;
- the 16-rank topology-slice reasoning behind all of the above.

A per-node hardware story is not excluded — `sg8txs64` also held a task in an earlier preempted
attempt — but it is no longer needed to explain anything.

## Reproduce

Model shape, from the faulting 4-rack `ctxext` W&B config, on `main` at `d7bddb0ad`:

```
hidden_dim 2048   num_layers 22   num_experts 128   top-k 4   num_shared_experts 2
num_heads 16   num_kv_heads 4   head_dim 128   intermediate_dim 1024
max_seq_len 65536   sliding_window 2048   capacity_factor 1.0
gpu_fa4_cute + sonic_cute   expert_chunks 1
1 rack, batch 64 -> 4.19M tokens/step
```

`main` has no launcher for this shape; I added it as a `--variant ctxext` on the FSDP hero launcher
(a config builder plus a CLI choice) and plumbed `max_task_failures` through
`dispatch_grug_training_run`, which hardcoded 10. Say the word if that is worth a PR rather than a
local branch.

```bash
RID=ii-repro-1rack-$(date -u +%Y%m%d-%H%M)
uv run --frozen iris --cluster=marin job run --no-wait --enable-extra-resources \
  --target-cluster cw-us-east-08a --priority production \
  --cpu 2 --memory 8GB --disk 32GB --timeout 86400 \
  --job-name "${RID}-coord" -e WANDB_API_KEY "$WANDB_API_KEY" -e JAX_ENABLE_PGLE 0 \
  -- python -m experiments.grug.moe_hero_fsdp.launch \
     --run-id "$RID" --dp-racks 1 --batch-size 64 --num-steps 500 \
     --variant ctxext --mode stock-control --no-save-checkpoints --version dev --run
```

`--mode stock-control` runs the plain entrypoint with `max_retries_failure=0`, so the faulting
attempt survives for inspection instead of warm-restarting from step 1.

**`-e JAX_ENABLE_PGLE 0` is required, and cost me two attempts to learn.** `HERO_FSDP_RUNTIME_ENV`
defaults `JAX_ENABLE_PGLE=1`; at this config that dies 28 s into training with
`jax.errors.JaxRuntimeError: ALREADY_EXISTS: Another profiling session active` in `train_step`, then
takes the gang on the same 300 s barrier and looks superficially like this issue. The faulting
`ctxext` runs had `enable_pgle: false`, so PGLE off is also the more faithful setting.

## Two traps for anyone reading these logs

**`CUDA_ERROR_CONTAINED` is not this issue.** The PGLE crash above produced 674 lines of
`cudaFreeAsync failed to free ...: CUDA_ERROR_CONTAINED: Invalid access of peer GPU memory over
nvlink`, single-rank, with the same allocator stats dump. It is teardown fallout: those lines are
timestamped *after* the barrier failure, whereas a real occurrence precedes it. Check the ordering
against the barrier, not the shape of the flood.

**The rate is low and this is not a reliable reproducer.** The same config on the same rack ran 500
steps clean an hour earlier (`ii-repro-1rack-20260811-0105`, 3.7 s/it), so it is 1 fault in 2 valid
attempts. Two earlier attempts were censored, one by preemption at step 163 and one by the PGLE
crash. Budget several runs.

## Control

`mhep-hero-d6144-sw2048-20T-10r-watch-20260810` ran on the same cluster across the same window:
10 racks, 640 GPUs, `gpu_fa4_cute` with `moe_implementation="fixed_all_to_all"`, 48 layers, d6144.
It reached step ~999 over ~14.2 h and was then killed by its owner, with zero signature at any point
(polled every 5 minutes for the whole run). That is roughly 9,000 GPU-hours of FA4 exposure without
`sonic_cute` and no fault, against a 64-GPU `sonic_cute` job that faulted 36 s in.

The low-exposure objection that applies to the rung-1 rows does not apply to that control. It is
still not a controlled comparison — model shape, sequence length, MoE kernel, and batch all differ
at once — and it ended by a kill rather than a fixed budget, so it does not settle `sonic_cute`.

## Divergences from the faulting 4-rack config

Recorded so nobody reads this as an exact transcription: `offload_opt_state=True` here versus
`False` there (the hero trainer sets it), and `qb_estimator` does not exist on `main` so
`qb_estimator=HIST` is not reproduced. Everything the `main` model config can express matches.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖 **Both of my 1-rack faults landed on the same GPU: `sg8txs64` device 0. Every run that did not draw that node ran clean.**

Second 1-rack reproduction, and this one carries the canonical error from the issue title, which my [first 1-rack fault](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7956#issuecomment-5256188981) did not show:

```
jax.errors.JaxRuntimeError: INTERNAL: Failed to retrieve branch_index value on stream 0xb20bc6e3b350:
  CUDA error: Could not synchronize CUDA stream:
  CUDA_ERROR_ILLEGAL_INSTRUCTION: an illegal instruction was encountered
```

| | |
|---|---|
| Run | `ii-unarmed-1rack-20260811-1900` |
| Onset | 2026-08-11 20:15:57.114 UTC, step ~166 |
| Faulting rank | iris task 14, local rank 0, **node `sg8txs64`** |
| Signature | 4166 lines, single rank; no other task emitted a CUDA error |
| Gang death | abort at 20:21:03, `failures=1`, `cosched_failed=15` |

## The node table

Eleven 1-rack runs of the same `ctxext` config, over 21 hours. `sg8txs64` is the only node that
distinguishes the faults from the clean runs.

| Run | `sg8txs64` in allocation | Outcome |
|---|---|---|
| `ii-repro-1rack-20260811-0105` | yes, task 14 | clean, 500/500 |
| `ii-repro-1rack-b-20260811-0215` | yes, task 14 | **fault on task 14** |
| `ii-unarmed-1rack-20260811-1900` | yes, task 14 | **fault on task 14** |
| `ii-repro-1rack-20260810-2335` | yes, task 13 | preempted — censored |
| `ii-repro-1rack-20260811-0020` | yes, task 14 | crashed on a PGLE profiling collision — censored |
| `ii-ctrl-scatter-1rack-20260811-1501` | no | clean, 500/500 |
| `ii-repro-1rack-dump-20260811-1500` | no | clean, 500/500 |
| `ii-dump-1rack-{a,b,c,d}-20260811` | no | clean, 500/500 each |

Both faults are the same node **and** the same device index on it. Fisher exact on the six valid
runs without the node (0 faults) against the three with it (2 faults) gives p ≈ 0.08.

## Why this is not "found the bad GPU"

- **The node is not sufficient.** `ii-repro-1rack-20260811-0105` ran 500 clean steps with
  `sg8txs64` as task 14. Something else has to coincide.
- **The fleet history contradicts a single bad device.** Faults in this thread have been recorded on
  at least ten distinct nodes — `sgzvxs64`, `s5trxs64`, `s8rrxs64`, `s38vxs64`, `s6xvxs64`,
  `sj1txs64`, `s7htxs64`, `s9xvxs64`, `sjwsxs64`, `sgd50t64`. One defective GPU cannot explain those.

What it is consistent with is a population of *marginal* devices, with a small 1-rack draw pool
repeatedly returning one of them. That moves "a GPU or driver-level fault not visible in node
labels" — open hypothesis 1 in the description — back up the ranking, and it makes the Xid
correlation this issue has wanted much more targeted: **two exact timestamps on one named node**,
02:30:45.245 and 20:15:57.114 UTC on 2026-08-11, both `sg8txs64`, both device 0.

## A confound worth publishing, because I nearly reported the opposite

I had been running attempts with CUDA device core dumps armed
(`CUDA_ENABLE_COREDUMP_ON_EXCEPTION=1`), and the armed runs went 0 faults in 5 while unarmed went 2
in 3. Given that `CUDA_LAUNCH_BLOCKING=1` is already known to suppress this fault, instrumentation
suppressing it was a live reading, and I was about to treat it as one.

It was allocation, not instrumentation: **all five armed runs happened to draw node sets without
`sg8txs64`**, because the node was held by another job for that whole window. Anyone comparing fault
rates across runs here should check node membership before attributing a difference to a knob.

## Still no core dump

A dump only gets written when a device exception occurs, and the two exceptions both landed on
unarmed runs — one predating the tooling, one the deliberate unarmed control. Five armed runs, two
faults, never the same run.

The arming and capture path is verified working end to end (uploader confirmed active on every rank,
writing to the run's output prefix); it has simply never been present at the moment of a fault. Iris
exposes no node-level placement constraint — `ResourceConfig` carries region/zone/cluster/device and
the K8s backend maps only `pool` and `region` — so I cannot currently aim an armed run at
`sg8txs64`. Suggestions welcome; otherwise the plan is to keep armed attempts running until one
draws the node.

## Config

Unchanged from the 1-rack recipe in my previous comment: d2048, 22 layers, 128 experts top-4 plus 2
shared, seq 65536, sliding window 2048, `gpu_fa4_cute` + `sonic_cute`, `expert_chunks=1`,
`replica_axis_size=1`, batch 64, `JAX_ENABLE_PGLE=0`, on `main` at `d7bddb0ad` plus the `ctxext`
launcher variant.

spillover_issues.author: rjpower
spillover_issues.body: We frequently run into issues with the wrong chat template being applied for a model between e.g. pre and post training. How can we adjust our abstractions so that this is less of an issue. Currently the template seems roughly tied to the tokenizer, but we've seen multiple locations where it needs to be supplied separately or adjusted. How do we adjust this?

comments.author: claude[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 # Research

The chat template has **two independent homes that are never reconciled**: the tokenizer artifact (`tokenizer_config.json` / `chat_template.jinja`) and a `chat_template` field re-declared at every consumer. Post-training reads the second but exports the first, so a checkpoint trained with template *X* ships template *Y*, and inference/eval then load *Y* from that checkpoint.

**The concrete drift** (SFT runs through `train_lm`):
- `LmDataConfig.the_tokenizer` returns `load_marin_tokenizer(self.tokenizer)` and **ignores `LmDataConfig.chat_template`** — [`datasets.py#L691-695`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/data/text/datasets.py#L691-L695) vs the field at [`datasets.py#L629`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/data/text/datasets.py#L629).
- The training template is consumed only inside the data processor to build masks — [`formats.py#L48-70`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/data/text/formats.py#L48-L70).
- HF export uses `tokenizer = config.data.the_tokenizer` and passes **no** `chat_template` to the export hooks — [`train_lm.py#L149`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/main/train_lm.py#L149), [`train_lm.py#L400-415`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/main/train_lm.py#L400-L415). `save_pretrained`/`_save_tokenizer_pretrained` *support* an override but nobody threads the training template in — [`hf_checkpoints.py#L1044-1076`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/compat/hf_checkpoints.py#L1044-L1076).

Net: the exported post-trained checkpoint carries the **base** tokenizer's template (or none), not the one the model was trained against.

**The proliferation** (each site re-specifies, falling back to the tokenizer independently, with no cross-check):
- `SFTSpec.chat_template` — *required* — [`launcher.py#L503`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/sft/launcher.py#L503)
- `ChatLmDatasetFormat`, `PreferenceChatLmDatasetFormat`, `TraceChatEvaluationFormat` each carry their own `chat_template`
- Inference: `ServeConfig.chat_template`, `ServedModelConfig.chat_template_content`, and vLLM `--chat-template`
- Templates are passed as **raw jinja strings** (`MARIN_CHAT_TEMPLATE`, `DELPHI_V0_CHAT_TEMPLATE`, `OPENCODE_TOOLS_CHAT_TEMPLATE`), so there is no identity/equality to detect drift — only the cache-key hash at [`launcher.py#L683`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/sft/launcher.py#L683) notices a change, and only for caching.

# Proposed approach

Make the **tokenizer the single source of truth** and let the training template travel with the checkpoint, so downstream never re-specifies unless deliberately overriding.

1. **Close the export hole (small, high-leverage).** Apply `LmDataConfig.chat_template` onto `the_tokenizer` via `with_chat_template` so the object used for masking *and* export is the same one. The `{% generation %}` block is standard HF syntax and is inert unless `return_assistant_tokens_mask=True`, so embedding the training template in the exported tokenizer is correct. This alone makes post-trained checkpoints self-describing and removes the most common footgun. Log a warning when the data template differs from the tokenizer's own.

2. **Default consumers to the checkpoint's template.** Inference/eval should read the template off the loaded tokenizer by default and treat `ServeConfig.chat_template` / `--chat-template` as an *explicit override that warns* on divergence — not a silent parallel source.

3. **Give templates identity (optional but recommended).** Replace raw-string passing with a small named `ChatTemplate` value (name + jinja + `has_generation_block`) plus a registry for the Marin/Delphi/Opencode templates. Equality then makes drift detectable (assert train == checkpoint == serve) instead of relying on a 6-char hash.

Recommendation: land (1) first as a focused change with a regression test that export-roundtrips a tiny model and asserts the exported `chat_template` equals the training template; treat (2) and (3) as follow-ups. This is architecturally significant and spans training→export→inference, so this is analysis rather than a PR — please confirm the direction (in particular whether (1) should also cover `train_dpo`/preference export) before implementation.

spillover_issues.body:
<!-- experiment-tldr:start -->
## Summary

This experiment is implementing two EP64 MoE routing changes in Levanter: MoonEP-style redundant-expert routing and global-histogram quantile balancing, motivated by PR #7890
s fast but dropping baseline (MHEP-004: 24.1231%% MFU with 9.6786%% drops). The correctness path now reaches zero assignment drops on one NVL72, but performance is far below the 21.7%% MFU gate: MNEP-095b reached 9.568%% MFU and MNEP-102 reached 9.937%% MFU. Profiling points at bounded-token all-to-all falling back to ragged transport (14.536s, 55.7%% communication), so the current blocker is token-transport efficiency rather than MoE math correctness. Separately, 64-GPU H100 QB ablations show global histogram improves balancing slightly with no observed loss gain and about a 1%% slowdown; unless new evidence appears, logits-domain histogram QB is the lower-risk direction to test on GB200.

### Helpful links
- [EP64 baseline PR #7890](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/7890)
- [MoonEP correctness and transport update](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7891#issuecomment-5169273360)
- [Ragged-kernel failure and bounded-collective decision](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7891#issuecomment-5158803255)
- [64-GPU QB ablation report](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/reports/QB-Ablations--VmlldzoxNzY0MjAxMA)
- [Experiment logbook snapshot](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/1c2015d4a/.agents/logbooks/7891-moonep-jax.md)
<!-- experiment-tldr:end -->

## Description

PR #7890 supplies the EP64 baseline. Its 25-step MHEP-004 run reached 24.1231% median MFU with 9.6786% final assignment drops. Its 200-step MHEP-008 run reached 23.6969% median MFU with 7.4113% final drops.

MoonEP balances compute with dynamic redundant experts. The Kimi K3 report also replaces per-rank quantile estimates with one global integer histogram reduction per layer and step.

## Hypothesis or Goal

A portable JAX MoonEP path can preserve forward and backward results and remove all assignment drops at EP64. Profile-based changes can recover at least 90% of the MHEP-004 median MFU.

The experiment matrix separates the changes:

* Fixed all-to-all with global histogram QB.
* MoonEP JAX with the current local QB.
* MoonEP JAX with global histogram QB.

## Status

The research branch starts at PR #7890 commit `e38ae4f8`. MoonEP correctness has passed zero-drop checks on one NVL72, but the current bounded-token path is still around 9.9% median MFU, below the 21.7% performance gate. The active follow-up is profiling and reducing token-transport overhead.

## Links

* Logbook: `.agents/logbooks/7891-moonep-jax.md`.
* W&B Report: Pending for the combined GB200 path.
* Important updates: #7279, #7890, https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24653, https://github.com/moonshotAI/moonep

## Decision Log

* 2026-08-02: Use a portable JAX correctness path before native CUDA fabric transport.
* 2026-08-02: Require zero assignment drops and at least 21.7% median MFU for the final combined run.
* 2026-08-03: Treat token transport as the main blocker after zero-drop NVL72 runs reached only about 9.9% median MFU.

## Conclusion

Correctness is proven for the exact MoonEP path on one NVL72, but the experiment has not met its performance gate. Continue with transport profiling and optimization before treating MoonEP plus global histogram QB as viable for the target EP64 path.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖 The ragged fallback in MNEP-096 has a cause in XLA, and two post-0.11.0 commits target it.

Read from the XLA revision jaxlib 0.11.0 pins, `131bf41acb4650e4391a640c3f1859c1c86ad74b` (2026-07-16), so all of this applies to the build MNEP has been running.

- At EP64 the peer-pointer one-shot kernel cannot be selected. `IsRaggedAllToAllKernelSupported` requires `num_outputs <= kMaxNumRaggedAllToAllOutputPtrs`, which is 8, and `num_outputs` is the replica-group size. A 64-rank group never qualifies. The remaining fast path is the NCCL-LSA one, gated on `lsa_size == clique_key.num_devices()`. Everything else falls through to a loop of `num_ranks * num_updates_per_replica` individual `ncclSend`/`ncclRecv` pairs, preceded by a device-to-host copy of the offset buffers and a `stream.BlockHostUntilDone()`. That fallback shape is consistent with the 14.536s and 55.7% communication share in MNEP-096, though I have not read your XProf trace to confirm which of the two it landed on.

- `--xla_gpu_experimental_ragged_all_to_all_use_device_kernel=true` is a no-op on its own. The kernel requires `FindSymmetricMemory` to return non-null for both the input and the output buffer (`ragged_all_to_all_thunk.cc`), and under the default `--xla_gpu_ragged_all_to_all_mode=private` both are null, so it falls through silently. XLA's own e2e test only ever instantiates that impl with `COLLECTIVES_SYMMETRIC_MEMORY`. Anyone testing it needs both flags.

- Two commits landed after 0.11.0's pin. `acb5aaffe` (2026-07-24) adds a device-initiated kernel on NCCL 2.29 LSA/GIN that runs the collective in a single launch, with the stated goal of eliminating per-call host coordination. `7e502c985` (2026-07-31) enables the multi-host decomposer by default for ragged-all-to-all spanning multiple LSA domains. The decomposer already exists in 0.11.0 as `--xla_gpu_unsupported_enable_ragged_all_to_all_multi_host_decomposer`, defaulted false, so it is testable today without a version change.

The `CUDA_ERROR_ILLEGAL_ADDRESS` in MNEP-017 is worth retesting against a nightly. I have no evidence it is fixed; the relevant kernel was substantially rewritten in that window.

I am starting a throughput A/B of these paths on the EP64 hero on branch `research/mcwitt/7201-ra2a-xla-ab`, comparing `fixed_all_to_all` against `ragged_all_to_all` bare, with the multi-host decomposer, with symmetric memory, and on a nightly jaxlib with the device kernel. It will use one rack per run for 25 steps. Happy to re-order or drop arms if that conflicts with the MNEP queue, and I will post the numbers here either way since the transport blocker looks shared.

comments.author: ravwojdyla-agent
comments.body:
🤖 Nsight Systems profile of the best reproducible configuration (MNEP-120)

Configuration is the MNEP-102 graph: exact MoonEP, global histogram QB, two token
buckets, compute-overlap schedule, ragged direct-device transport, and the
one-remote-CTA wheel. The hook profiles task zero only, which covers its four GPUs.
Report and SQLite export:

- `s3://marin-us-east-02a/tmp/ttl=30d/iris-profiles/rav/mnep-120-best-config-nsys-5-20260804-0620-coord/.../r00000-s1nrxs64.nsys-rep`
- `s3://marin-us-east-02a/tmp/ttl=30d/rav/nsysexport/r00000.sqlite`

## Read the step-level numbers with care

Nsight tracing costs a lot at this kernel count. The profiled step takes `51.55 s`
against `26.17 s` for the same configuration without a profiler, and the trace shows
`58%` GPU idle against `6%` in the XProf trace of the same graph. The device-side
per-kernel times agree with XProf, so use those. Do not use the step totals or the
idle fraction from this report.

## Kernel time for each step, device 0

| class | s for each step | share |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ragged transport | 11.95 | 47.9% |
| other | 3.91 | 15.7% |
| expert GEMM (QuACK) | 3.21 | 12.9% |
| dense GEMM | 2.56 | 10.3% |
| MoE layout (sonic) | 1.66 | 6.6% |
| attention | 1.34 | 5.4% |
| NCCL collectives | 0.33 | 1.3% |

## The transport splits into two different problems

864 ragged calls run on each GPU in each step. The durations are bimodal.

| call type | count | median | bytes | rate |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| token dispatch and combine | 1,968 in 5 steps | `24.14 ms` | `2.685 GB` | `111.2 GB/s` |
| expert weight exchange | 2,352 in 5 steps | `3.14 ms` | small | `9.5 GB/s` |

The token path is bandwidth-limited. The weight path is latency-limited: it carries
`22.65 GB` for each step, which is `1.46%` of the `1,546 GB` of token traffic, but it
uses `20%` of all ragged time. The weight exchange sends `w13` `[4,5120,2560]` and `w2`
`[4,1280,5120]` for up to four copied experts in each layer, in three passes, which is
288 small transfers for each step. Batching those calls looks like a cheap gain of
about `2.4 s` for each step.

## Two candidate causes that the profile rejects

Host launch behavior is not a limit. The delay from the launch call to the kernel start
is `48.95 ms` at p50 and `213.9 ms` at p90, so the host runs ahead of the device. The
200,770 kernel launches in each step do not gate the step.

Memory contention is not a limit. The trace holds 136,268 device-to-device copies that
move `7,818 GB` across five steps, but only `7.8 GB` of that overlaps a ragged kernel,
which is `0.1 GB/s` of competing demand. XLA schedules those copies outside the
collective.

Transport overlaps compute for `27%` of its wall time.

## The open question

The same kernel gives `106` to `111 GB/s` in training and `305` to `335 GB/s` in an
isolated benchmark at the same peer message size. Two profilers and two runs agree on
the training figure.

Measured and rejected as the cause: message size (`9%` across an eight-times change),
message skew (`21%`), expert GEMM contention (no measurable cost), the collective
overlap limit (raising it was slower), rank count 16 to 32 (no loss), rank arrival skew
(host medians agree to `0.5 ms`), host CPU count (`6.9%` from 8 to 32 CPUs), and now
launch behavior and memory contention.

Current hypothesis: the kernel launches with `grid:64,1,1` for every rank count. That
gives about four CTAs to each peer at 16 ranks and about one CTA to each peer at 64
ranks. Every earlier test held rank count at 16 or 32. MNEP-124 runs the benchmark at
64 ranks to test this.

spillover_issues.author: rfgordan
spillover_issues.body:
Picks up item 16 (robustness to prompt noise and irrelevant context) of #7090,
covering both axes in one chat-mode GSM8K eval.

**Revised design (2026-08-04).** Supersedes the original zeroeval-based plan
after implementation and multi-model validation. What changed and why:

- **Standalone benchmark (`GSM8KPerturbed`), not a zeroeval extension.** No
  zeroeval task is in the canonical campaign (#7505), and wiring into it
  surfaced unexercised-code bugs. A self-contained directory matches the
  checked-in-data convention of the canonical Tier-2 benchmarks.
- **Data sourced from openai/gsm8k only**, replacing the third-party
  zero-eval mirror (content verified identical).
- **Static realization checked in**: both data files are committed and open
  with a meta line recording the exact generation command, seed, and
  parameters. Runs are fully offline; regeneration is byte-identical.
- **lm-eval zero-shot protocol**: the "Question:/Answer:" prompt through the
  chat template, graded by flexible-extract (last number) — the exact
  protocol of the prior Marin chat-mode GSM8K measurement (#7321).
- **Paired evaluation.** Per-condition metrics grade each perturbed instance
  against the clean run of the same item; comparing against overall clean
  accuracy conflated perturbation effects with item-subset difficulty
  (+/-5-8pp observed, fabricating effects in both directions).
- **Off-domain history (oasst2), not GSM8K train exchanges.** Same-domain
  history was measurably confounded: solved exemplars acted as few-shot
  demonstrations and *improved* weak-model accuracy (+6.7 paired delta at 4
  exchanges on gpt-3.5-turbo). Off-domain chat flipped the same condition to
  genuine dose-responsive degradation (-6.7 at 4, -11.0 at 16).
- **Per-condition no-answer rate** is a first-class metric: it separates
  cannot-solve from cannot-format, and exposes infrastructure failures
  recorded as outputs (which once fabricated a spurious 28-point
  "collapse").

## Goal

(unchanged) Response quality should be insensitive to user-prompting
imprecision (whitespace, linebreaks, typos) and to irrelevant prior context.
Measure how much chat-mode GSM8K accuracy a model conserves under each,
against a same-protocol clean reference.

## Conditions

Eight conditions, one per test item (~165 items each), seeded and
reproducible. Noise conditions rewrite only the question text; history
conditions leave it verbatim and prepend prior chat turns.

| condition    | type    | what it does                                      |
|--------------|---------|---------------------------------------------------|
| misspellings | noise   | dictionary misspellings, p=0.2 per eligible word  |
| lowercase    | noise   | lowercases the whole question                     |
| extra_space  | noise   | multiplies spaces between words (1-3)             |
| typos        | noise   | keyboard-adjacent character swaps, p=0.05         |
| homophones   | noise   | CMUdict exact-homophone swaps, p=0.1 per word     |
| mild_mix     | noise   | HELM's composite: lowercase + contract + misspell + respace |
| history_4    | history | 4 unrelated oasst2 chat exchanges prepended       |
| history_16   | history | 16 unrelated oasst2 chat exchanges prepended      |

Notes:
- The first four noise transforms and mild_mix are byte-identical to HELM's
  invariance perturbations under a shared RNG.
- homophones models voice-transcription input and may swap spelled-out
  number words (two -> too); those items are flagged in metadata as
  recoverable-from-context.
- History exchanges (OpenAssistant/oasst2 root prompt + best reply,
  length-bounded, unfiltered; 2.1% math-adjacent) are embedded verbatim in
  the data file with source message ids; sampling is seeded independently
  of item content.
- Dropped from v1: standalone contraction (84% no-op on GSM8K prose), the
  middle misspelling dose, and the 2/8/32 history ladder (now 4/16).

## Metrics

Per condition, all paired against the clean run of the same items: accuracy,
clean-subset accuracy, paired delta, harmed/helped flip counts, and
no-answer rate; plus changed-only and spoken-number slices, and clean-arm
accuracy/no-answer overall.

## Implementation

eval/chat_benchmarks/GSM8KPerturbed/ in the Evalchemy fork:

- eval_instruct.py — loader, chat construction, grading, paired per-condition metrics
- src/perturbations.py — transforms, byte-parity-verified against HELM's code
- data_prep/generate.py — regenerates the committed data files
- data/gsm8k_clean.jsonl, data/gsm8k_perturbed.jsonl — the static realization

spillover_issues.body:
<!-- experiment-tldr:start -->
## Summary

This issue started as a proposal to add five supervised target-only synthetic perplexity probes for surface-form grammars where Qwen3 32B appeared to beat Marin 32B: delimiter/table formats, identifier and encoding strings, machine records and configs, patch/diff surfaces, and science/markup/tree-closure formats. The initial blocker was that the repo did not yet have the supervised target-only scoring path or all-available diagnostic entrypoint, but those pieces were later implemented. The five probe families were uploaded to Hugging Face with pinned revisions, added to the v18 all-available perplexity-gap run, and scored in the refreshed dashboard. The final readout found mixed gaps: Qwen was ahead on science/markup and machine-record subsets such as SDF closure, Dockerfiles, GitHub Actions logs, and nginx logs, while Marin was ahead on several identifier/escaping and whitespace-control subsets. The families were then archived as diagnostic probes in five closed follow-up experiment issues and long-lived research branches, not promoted as regular eval-suite entries.

### Helpful links
- https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/5618#issuecomment-4422651718
- https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/5618#issuecomment-4423585707
- https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/5618#issuecomment-4427592233
- #5659, #5660, #5661, #5662, #5663
<!-- experiment-tldr:end -->

## Motivation
The v17b Marin 32B vs Qwen3 32B perplexity-gap dashboard suggests that several remaining non-multilingual gaps are surface-form grammar gaps rather than broad prose/reasoning gaps. Qwen's durable edges cluster around rigid technical serialization formats: IDs, logs, configs, SVG/XML, bio/chem records, diffs, and dense structured rows.

This issue tracks a batch of supervised target-only synthetic PPL probe families intended to test those hypotheses independently. These are base-model continuation formats, not chat-framed prompts.

## Probe families

- Delimiters / whitespace / table formats: TSV, CSV, pipes, fixed-width columns, Markdown tables, aligned spaces, Makefile tabs, Python indentation.
- Identifier / encoding grammars: package/version strings, commit hashes, UUID/build IDs, accessions, mixed-case symbolic IDs, base64/data URI, hex dumps, URL escaping, JSON escapes.
- Machine records / configs: Zeek/nginx/k8s/system logs, tracebacks/compiler errors, GitHub Actions logs, JSON application logs, package.json, pyproject, Actions YAML, Dockerfile, Terraform, Kubernetes YAML.
- Patch/diff / agent-readiness surfaces: unified diffs, file path + line references, review comment threads, failing-test-to-patch traces, commit metadata, GitHub PR event patches.
- Science / markup / tree closure: SMILES/SDF/PDB/mmCIF/FASTA/GenBank-ish records, BibTeX/LaTeX, XML/HTML/SVG/MathML closure, entity escaping.

## Dataset shape

Each family should publish an HF dataset with one config per subset. Rows should include:

- `input`
- `target`
- `id`
- `subset`
- `task`
- `seed`
- `metadata`

Scoring should use supervised target-only loss via `supervised_text_dataset(..., input_key="input", target_key="target")`.

## Integration

- Add provider modules under `experiments/evals/`.
- Add the providers to `exp_model_perplexity_gap_all_available_diag.py` after each HF dataset is uploaded and pinned.
- Use the per-dataset score cache so future dashboard runs only score the new/changed subsets.
- Add heatmap groups for these families if the aggregate rows expose interesting gaps.

Parent epic: #5005.

# Research

This issue spans five probe families (delimiters/tables, identifiers/encodings, machine records/configs, patch/diff, science/markup) — each with ~5-10 subsets that need an HF dataset constructed and pinned. Scope is well beyond a single self-contained PR. Two prerequisites referenced in the issue body do not exist yet in the repo, so a parallel implementation PR would also be premature:

- No `supervised_text_dataset(..., input_key=\"input\", target_key=\"target\")` exists. Current scoring path is text-only: [`perplexity_gap.py#L48-L55`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/perplexity_gap.py#L48-L55) defines \`RawTextEvaluationDataset\` with a single \`text_key\`, and [`raw_text_dataset`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/perplexity_gap.py#L84-L101) only emits raw-text datasets. There is no supervised target-only loss path in \`lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/\` or in levanter (grep for \`input_key\`/\`target_key\` returns nothing relevant).
- No \`exp_model_perplexity_gap_all_available_diag.py\` integration file. The closest existing entrypoints are [`exp_model_perplexity_gap_marin_vs_llama.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/exp_model_perplexity_gap_marin_vs_llama.py), [`exp_model_perplexity_gap_long_tail_runnable.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/exp_model_perplexity_gap_long_tail_runnable.py), [`exp_model_perplexity_gap_fineweb2_multilingual.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/exp_model_perplexity_gap_fineweb2_multilingual.py), and [`exp_model_perplexity_gap_coverage_matrix.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/exp_model_perplexity_gap_coverage_matrix.py). The bundle/model/pair plumbing in [`perplexity_gap_registry.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/evals/perplexity_gap_registry.py) is keyed on \`PerplexityGapBundle\` with a \`datasets_factory: () -> dict[str, RawTextEvaluationDataset]\`, i.e. raw-text only.

Sibling issues are still open and overlap the design surface: #5056 (raw web/markup/image-text PPL — same registration pattern), #4963 (chat / agent / numeracy supervised-ish PPL — already proposes target-only conditional likelihood). #4963 in particular should drive the supervised target-only API; this issue should layer on top once that lands.

**Relevant code**
- [`perplexity_gap.py#L48-L101`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/perplexity_gap.py#L48-L101) - raw-text-only dataset abstraction
- [`perplexity_gap_registry.py#L40-L102`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/evals/perplexity_gap_registry.py#L40-L102) - bundle/factory contract is \`dict[str, RawTextEvaluationDataset]\`
- [`gh_archive_structured_output.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/evals/gh_archive_structured_output.py) - canonical pattern for per-family provider modules
- [`long_tail_ppl.py#L29-L65`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/evals/long_tail_ppl.py#L29-L65) - existing slice registry pattern (StrEnum family + dataclass slice + registry_key)
- Parent epic: #5005; sibling: #5056, #4963

# Proposed Approach (no PR, human review needed)

The work is too large and too unfounded for a single agent PR (>>100 LOC across new evaluation infra, ~30+ provider entries, new datasets, an absent integration file). Recommend splitting before implementation:

1. **First, land supervised target-only scoring infra in #4963 or a dedicated infra issue.** Add a \`SupervisedTextEvaluationDataset(input_key, target_key, hf_dataset_id, hf_dataset_name, split, tags)\` alongside \`RawTextEvaluationDataset\` in [`perplexity_gap.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/perplexity_gap.py), plumb a \`model_supervised_perplexity_scores\` step through levanter that masks loss to \`target\` tokens, and extend \`PerplexityGapBundle\` to accept either dataset variant. Without this, every family in #5618 is blocked.

2. **Split #5618 into five sub-issues, one per family** (delimiters/tables, identifier/encoding grammars, machine records/configs, patch/diff/agent-readiness, science/markup/tree closure). Each sub-issue tracks: HF dataset construction with the \`(input, target, id, subset, task, seed, metadata)\` schema, the provider module under \`experiments/evals/\`, and registration into a new \`exp_model_perplexity_gap_all_available_diag.py\` once the infra in (1) lands. Each sub-issue should fit in a PR-sized chunk and can run independently.

3. **Add the integration entrypoint as its own small PR** once at least one family is uploaded: a thin \`exp_model_perplexity_gap_all_available_diag.py\` that aggregates the existing bundles + new supervised bundles via \`build_registered_perplexity_gap_coverage_plan\`, mirroring \`exp_model_perplexity_gap_coverage_matrix.py\`.

Out of scope for any single agent PR: constructing and uploading HF datasets (needs human curation, licensing review, and HF org credentials), and choosing which subsets/sources are worth materializing first.

If a maintainer wants me to take a first concrete slice — recommend starting with the supervised target-only API change (item 1), which is bounded and unblocks everything else. Flag here and I will scope a PR against #4963.
